title: No. 70 — The Executive Department Further Considered (Hamilton)
paragraphs: There is an idea, not without its supporters, that a vigorous Executive is inconsistent with the spirit of republican government. Enlightened well-wishers of this form of government must at least hope that this assumption has no foundation. They can never admit its truth without simultaneously condemning their own principles. Energy in the Executive is a defining feature of good government. It is essential to protecting the community against foreign attacks. It is no less essential to the steady administration of the laws; to protecting property against those irregular and high-handed combinations that sometimes interrupt the ordinary course of justice; to securing liberty against the schemes and assaults of ambition, faction, and anarchy. Anyone the least familiar with Roman history knows how often that republic had to take refuge in the absolute power of a single man, under the formidable title of Dictator. This was needed against the intrigues of ambitious individuals who aimed at tyranny, against the seditions of whole classes whose conduct threatened the existence of all government, and against external enemies who menaced Rome with conquest and destruction.

There is no need, however, to multiply arguments or examples on this point. A feeble Executive implies a feeble execution of the government. A feeble execution is just another phrase for bad execution. And a government badly executed, whatever it may be in theory, must in practice be a bad government.

Taking it for granted, then, that all sensible people will agree on the necessity of an energetic Executive, the only remaining question is: what are the ingredients that constitute this energy? How far can they be combined with the other ingredients that constitute safety in the republican sense? And how far does the convention's reported plan show this combination?
The ingredients that constitute energy in the Executive are: first, unity; second, duration; third, adequate provision for its support; fourth, competent powers.
The ingredients that constitute safety in the republican sense are: first, due dependence on the people; second, due responsibility.

The politicians and statesmen most celebrated for the soundness of their principles and the justice of their views have come down in favor of a single Executive and a numerous legislature. They have rightly considered energy as the most necessary qualification of the former, and have regarded this as most applicable to power in a single hand. They have, with equal correctness, considered the latter as best suited to deliberation and wisdom, and best calculated to win the confidence of the people and secure their privileges and interests.

That unity contributes to energy will not be disputed. Decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch will generally mark the proceedings of one man much more than those of any larger number. As the number is increased, these qualities will diminish.

This unity may be destroyed in two ways: either by vesting power in two or more magistrates of equal dignity and authority, or by vesting it nominally in one man who is in whole or in part subject to the control and cooperation of others acting as his counselors. For the first, the two Consuls of Rome serve as an example. For the second, we find examples in the constitutions of several states. New York and New Jersey, if I remember correctly, are the only states that have entrusted executive authority entirely to single men.(1) Both methods of destroying the unity of the Executive have their advocates, but supporters of an executive council are more numerous. Both are open, if not to equal, then to similar objections, and may in most respects be examined together.

The experience of other nations offers little instruction on this point. As far as it teaches anything, it teaches us not to be enamored of plurality in the Executive. We have seen that the Achaeans, after experimenting with two Praetors, were led to abolish one. Roman history records many instances of harm to the republic from disagreements between the Consuls, and between the military Tribunes who were sometimes substituted for the Consuls. But it offers no example of any particular advantage gained by the state from the plurality of those magistrates. That the disagreements between them were not more frequent or more disastrous is astonishing — until we consider the unique position the republic was almost continually in, and the prudent policy, suggested by the state's circumstances and pursued by the Consuls, of dividing the government between them. The patricians were engaged in a perpetual struggle with the plebeians for the preservation of their ancient authorities and dignities. The Consuls, generally chosen from the patrician body, were commonly united by their personal interest in defending the privileges of their order. In addition to this motive for union, after the republic's arms had greatly expanded its empire, it became established custom for the Consuls to divide the administration between themselves by lot — one remained at Rome to govern the city and its surroundings, while the other took command in the more distant provinces. This arrangement must have had great influence in preventing the collisions and rivalries that might otherwise have disturbed the peace of the republic.

But leaving the dim light of historical research and turning purely to the dictates of reason and good sense, we shall find far more cause to reject than to approve the idea of plurality in the Executive, in any form whatever.

Wherever two or more persons are engaged in any common enterprise or pursuit, there is always a danger of difference of opinion. If they are clothed with equal dignity and authority in a public trust or office, there is special danger of personal rivalry and even animosity. From any of these causes, and especially from all of them combined, the most bitter dissensions tend to arise. When they happen, they reduce the respectability, weaken the authority, and disrupt the plans and operations of those they divide. If such dissensions should unfortunately strike the supreme executive magistracy of a country composed of multiple persons, they could obstruct or frustrate the most important measures of government in the state's most critical emergencies. And what is even worse, they could split the community into the most violent and irreconcilable factions, each adhering to a different individual on the magistracy.

People often oppose a thing simply because they had no hand in planning it, or because it may have been planned by those they dislike. But if they have been consulted and have happened to disapprove, opposition then becomes, in their view, an indispensable duty of self-love. They seem to think themselves bound by honor and by every motive of personal infallibility to defeat what has been resolved upon contrary to their views. People of upright, benevolent temperaments have too many opportunities to observe with horror how desperate this disposition can become. They see how often the great interests of society are sacrificed to the vanity, conceit, and obstinacy of individuals who have enough credit to make their passions and caprices matter to the rest of mankind. Perhaps the question now before the public will, in its consequences, provide melancholy proof of the effects of this contemptible weakness — or rather detestable vice — in the human character.

On the principles of a free government, the inconveniences from the source just mentioned must necessarily be accepted in the formation of the legislature. But it is unnecessary, and therefore unwise, to introduce them into the constitution of the Executive. It is here, too, that they may be most harmful. In the legislature, promptness of decision is more often an evil than a benefit. Differences of opinion and clashes of parties in that branch, though they may sometimes obstruct beneficial plans, often promote deliberation and caution and serve to check excesses by the majority. And once a resolution is taken, opposition must end. That resolution is law, and resistance to it is punishable. But no favorable circumstances mitigate or atone for the disadvantages of dissension in the executive department. Here, they are pure and unmixed. There is no point at which they cease to operate. They serve to embarrass and weaken the execution of any plan or measure they touch, from the first step to its final conclusion. They constantly counteract the qualities most necessary in the Executive — vigor and dispatch — and do so without any compensating good. In the conduct of war, where the energy of the Executive is the bulwark of national security, everything would be at risk from its plurality.

It must be admitted that these observations apply with chief weight to the first case supposed — a plurality of magistrates with equal dignity and authority — a scheme whose advocates are unlikely to form a numerous group. But they apply, though with less force, with considerable weight to the proposal of a council whose concurrence is constitutionally required for the operations of the nominal Executive. A skillful cabal in such a council could distract and weaken the entire system of administration. Even if no such cabal existed, mere diversity of views and opinions would be enough to color the exercise of executive authority with a spirit of habitual feebleness and delay.

(But one of the weightiest objections to a plurality in the Executive — applying as much to the second plan as to the first — is that it tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility. Responsibility is of two kinds: to censure and to punishment. The first is the more important of the two, especially in an elective office. A man in public trust will far more often act in ways that make him unworthy of further trust than in ways that make him liable to legal punishment. But multiplying the Executive adds to the difficulty of detection in either case. Amid mutual accusations, it often becomes impossible to determine on whom the blame or punishment for a harmful measure, or series of harmful measures, ought really to fall. It is shifted from one to another with such dexterity, and under such plausible appearances, that public opinion is left in suspense about the real author. The circumstances that may have led to any national failure or misfortune are sometimes so complicated that, where there are several actors who may have had different degrees and kinds of involvement, we may clearly see overall that there has been mismanagement — yet it may be impossible to say to whose account the harm should truly be charged.)(E1)

"I was overruled by my council. The council were so divided in their opinions that no better resolution on the point could be obtained." These and similar pretexts are constantly at hand, whether true or false. And who will take the trouble, or risk the unpopularity, of strict scrutiny into the secret springs of the transaction? Even if a citizen zealous enough to undertake this thankless task were found, if collusion exists between the parties involved, how easy it is to dress the circumstances in such ambiguity that the precise conduct of any of the parties remains uncertain.

In the single instance where the governor of this state is paired with a council — that is, in appointing to offices — we have seen the harm of such an arrangement in exactly the way now under consideration. Scandalous appointments to important offices have been made. Some cases have been so flagrant that ALL PARTIES have agreed on the impropriety. When inquiry was made, the blame was laid by the governor on the members of the council, who in turn pinned it on his nomination. The people remain entirely at a loss to determine by whose influence their interests have been committed to hands so unqualified and so plainly improper. Out of consideration for individuals, I refrain from going into particulars.

It is clear from these considerations that plurality of the Executive tends to deprive the people of the two greatest securities they can have for the faithful exercise of any delegated power. First, the restraints of public opinion, which lose their effect both because the censure for bad measures is divided among many, and because of the uncertainty about on whom it should fall. Second, the opportunity to detect, easily and clearly, the misconduct of the persons they trust, so they may either be removed from office or actually punished where the case allows.

In England, the king is a perpetual magistrate. By a maxim adopted for the sake of public peace, he is unaccountable for his administration and his person is sacred. Nothing, therefore, can be wiser in that kingdom than to attach to the king a constitutional council that may be answerable to the nation for the advice it gives. Without this, there would be no responsibility whatever in the executive department — an idea inadmissible in a free government. But even there the king is not bound by the resolutions of his council, though they are answerable for the advice they give. He is the absolute master of his own conduct in the exercise of his office and may observe or disregard the counsel given him entirely at his discretion.

But in a republic, where every magistrate ought to be personally responsible for his conduct in office, the reason that in the British Constitution recommends a council not only no longer applies but actually argues against the institution. In the monarchy of Great Britain, the council provides a substitute for the chief magistrate's prohibited responsibility, serving in some degree as a hostage to national justice for his good behavior. In the American republic, it would serve to destroy, or greatly diminish, the intended and necessary responsibility of the Chief Magistrate himself.

The idea of a council to the Executive, so widespread in the state constitutions, was derived from that maxim of republican jealousy which considers power safer in the hands of a number of men than in those of a single man. Even if the maxim were granted to apply here, I would contend that the advantage on that side would not outweigh the numerous disadvantages on the other. But I do not think the rule applies at all to the executive power. On this point I clearly agree with a writer whom the celebrated Junius pronounces "deep, solid, and ingenious" — that "the executive power is more easily confined when it is ONE";(2) that it is far safer to have a single object for the jealousy and watchfulness of the people; and, in a word, that all multiplication of the Executive is more dangerous than helpful to liberty.

A little reflection will convince us that the kind of security sought in multiplying the Executive cannot be achieved. Numbers must be so great as to make combination difficult, or they are a source of danger rather than security. The combined credit and influence of several individuals must be more formidable to liberty than the credit and influence of any one of them separately. When power, therefore, is placed in the hands of so small a number that their interests and views can easily be combined in a common enterprise by a skillful leader, it becomes more liable to abuse, and more dangerous when abused, than if it were lodged in the hands of one man. The single individual, by the very fact of being alone, will be more closely watched and more readily suspected, and cannot unite as much influence as when he is joined with others. The Decemvirs of Rome, whose name denotes their number,(3) were more to be feared in their usurpation than any ONE of them would have been. No one would propose an Executive much more numerous than that body; six to twelve have been suggested as the size of the council. Even the upper end of these numbers is not too large for easy combination, and from such a combination America would have more to fear than from the ambition of any single individual. A council to a magistrate who is himself responsible for what he does is generally nothing better than a drag on his good intentions, is often the instrument and accomplice of his bad ones, and is almost always a cloak for his faults.

I refrain from dwelling on the subject of expense, though it is plain that if the council were numerous enough to answer the main end of the institution, the salaries of members — who would have to be drawn from their homes to reside at the seat of government — would be too serious an item in the catalog of public expenditures to incur for an object of doubtful utility. I will only add that before the Constitution appeared, I rarely met an intelligent man from any of the states who did not admit, as the result of experience, that the UNITY of the executive of this state was one of the best distinguishing features of our constitution.

1. New York has no council except for the single purpose of appointing to offices. New Jersey has a council whom the governor may consult. But I think, from the terms of the constitution, their resolutions do not bind him.
2. De Lolme.
